speaker_role: current admissions interviewer (Yale Alumni Schools Committee volunteer)
commercial_incentive: None evident - personal channel, no services promoted
key_insights: Declining to opt into an interview, or not being offered one due to regional volunteer availability, does not affect the admissions decision at all - interviews are opportunistic, not guaranteed or required, and purely based on alumni volunteer supply in a given region

A strong interview can result in the interviewer writing a positive report that provides additional context to the admissions office, but it carries much less weight than the rest of the application (transcript, recommendations, essays)

Recommends journaling in advance about specific academic interests and extracurricular engagement (why they matter, how they've been pursued) so answers come across natural and authentic rather than rehearsed
Advises choosing interview format (video call vs. in-person) based on genuine personal comfort/strengths, not a perceived strategic advantage, since neither format is inherently favored
Recommends demonstrating fit organically by naturally reflecting the school's known cultural qualities (he cites Yale's 'intellectual curiosity') through genuine answers rather than performing them
States that applicants who stood out most were those who asked thoughtful, well-researched questions and displayed genuine enthusiasm and open-mindedness about the school
Explicitly warns against physical over-familiarity with the interviewer as an obvious don't
notable_or_distinctive: First-person account from an actual current Yale alumni interviewer describing exactly what he personally weighs and reports on, including confirmation that skipping the interview has zero effect on outcomes - a specific reassurance not always stated plainly in generic interview-tips content.
reliability_notes: Reflects one individual volunteer interviewer's personal approach and opinions at one institution (Yale); his personal practices (what he reports, what stands out to him) may not represent official Yale policy or other interviewers' approaches, and the casual/humorous tone (including an anecdote about nearly kissing an interviewer) should be read as personal color rather than universal guidance.
